background: In November 2026, an unauthorised party claimed to have obtained data from the music distributor for independent artists, Too Lost. The data contained 724k unique email addresses belonging to artists, their collaborators and fans.

Some records also contained bcrypt password hashes, while a small subset included partial credit card data (last 4 digits and card type), identity verification information (in some cases, passport, driver's licence or national ID numbers), and payouts made to artists. Too Lost advised that its investigation remains ongoing, external forensic specialists have been engaged, and measures have been taken to secure affected systems and credentials.
The company is also working with advisors to coordinate communications and support for affected individuals.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 724,323 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.

The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Driver's licenses, Email addresses, Government issued IDs, IP addresses, Names, Partial credit card data, Passport numbers, Passwords, Payment histories, Physical addresses, Places of birth, Social media profiles, Usernames.

fields.name: Government issued IDs
fields.why: Passport and licence numbers are used to prove identity to banks and telecoms, and they are effectively permanent.

fields.name: Passwords
fields.why: Anyone reusing this password elsewhere has those accounts exposed too, credential stuffing is automated and tries them all within days.

fields.name: Physical addresses
fields.why: Where someone actually lives. Combined with a name this moves the risk off the internet.

fields.name: Dates of birth
fields.why: One of the three things call centres ask to verify identity, and it never changes.

fields.name: Partial credit card data
fields.why: Not enough to spend, but enough to convince a victim that a caller is genuinely from their bank.

fields.name: Payment histories
fields.why: Shows what someone buys and from whom, the detail that makes a phishing message land.

fields.name: IP addresses
fields.why: Approximate location at the time of use, and a way to correlate accounts across services.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: An exposed address may be used in phishing attempts. Treat unexpected messages with caution.

fields.name: Usernames
fields.why: A matching handle can be a lead to other profiles, but does not prove shared ownership.

fields.name: Driver's licenses
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

fields.name: Passport numbers
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

fields.name: Places of birth
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

fields.name: Social media profiles
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

actions: Change this password anywhere you reused it, starting with your email account, that is the one that can reset all the others.
Check statements for the months after the breach date and ask your bank for a replacement card if the number was full.
Consider a credit freeze. A government identifier cannot be changed, so limiting what can be opened in your name is the only real control.
Be sceptical of post and callers who already know your address, knowing it is no longer evidence of anything.
Be alert to phishing. A message may use details from exposed or collected records to appear familiar; verify requests through the service directly.
